claims.claim: Pronouns are words that substitute for (stand in for) nouns or noun phrases, letting a writer avoid repeating the same noun.
Personal pronouns have subject forms (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) used in subject position and object forms (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) used as the object of a verb or preposition.

Possessive forms show ownership in two positions: possessive pronouns such as mine, yours, hers, ours, and theirs stand alone, while possessive determiners such as my, your, her, our, and their appear before a noun.

Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves) end in -self or -selves and are used when the object of a verb refers to the same person or thing as the subject; they should not replace ordinary object pronouns such as me or her.
The demonstrative pronouns this, that, these, and those point directly at specific people or things; the same four words can also function as determiners before a noun.
Indefinite pronouns such as someone, everybody, everything, and none refer to people or things that are not specific or not named.

Relative pronouns such as who, which, and that introduce clauses that connect back to a noun: who typically refers to people, which to animals and things, and that to people, animals, or things in informal use; full clause structure is treated in the sentence-structure topic.

A pronoun must agree with its antecedent (the noun it replaces) in number and, where the language marks it, gender, and the reference must be clear; a vague it or they that could refer to more than one noun is a common writing problem, fixed by naming the noun or rebuilding the sentence.
They and their are now widely used as singular, gender-neutral pronouns, a usage recognized by major style guides including the Associated Press and the Chicago Manual of Style.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Grammar frameworks classify possessive forms differently: OpenStax lists my, mine, your, yours and so on together under the possessive case, while other frameworks call my/your/her determiners (or adjectives) and reserve the label pronoun for forms that stand alone (mine, yours).
positions: Possessive case includes both my and mine (OpenStax, Purdue OWL table format).
Possessive pronouns stand alone while my/your/her appear before a noun (standard determiner analysis).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both sets of forms and explains the difference by position (before a noun versus standing alone), using the terms possessive determiner and possessive pronoun, without claiming one classification is the only correct one.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Singular they is a usage point, not a settled rule in every style tradition.
positions: They/their is increasingly used as singular and gender-neutral, recognized by AP and Chicago (Purdue OWL).
Some older prescriptive guides required he or he or she for singular antecedents.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson notes that singular they is widely accepted and treats the choice as context- and audience-sensitive, consistent with the subject's context-sensitive framing caution.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Relative pronoun choice (who/which/that) varies with formality and with whether the clause is defining or non-defining.
positions: That is used informally for people, animals, and things; who for people; which for animals and things (Cambridge Dictionary).
Defining versus non-defining clauses can restrict which relative pronoun is preferred (Cambridge Dictionary, separate page).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names who, which, and that as connectors and gives the simple who/which/that pattern, explicitly deferring clause structure to the sentence-structure topic.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft defined the topic circularly as 'a foundational Languages & Esl concept' and claimed 'College courses use pronouns as a building block' without evidence; no draft wording was supported and all of it was discarded.
The draft presented pronouns as a generic concept to 'apply to a scenario' rather than as a word class with named families and rules; this framing was not used.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generated boilerplate with source-verified content on pronoun families, case, possessive forms, and antecedent agreement.

Corrected the draft's generic application framing: the lesson now teaches specific, verifiable grammar claims (subject/object case, reflexive conditions of use, demonstrative/indefinite/relative families, agreement and clarity).
Clarified the my/mine distinction by position, following the determiner-versus-pronoun analysis, instead of lumping all possessive forms together.

sourceRecords.title: 20.6 Editing Focus: Pronouns — Writing Guide with Handbook
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Existing registry record reused with identical id and URL; read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: pronouns as substitutes for nouns/noun phrases; reference (gender and number matching); antecedent definition; case (subjective/objective/possessive) with the full personal-pronoun form tables; reflexive pronouns (-self/-selves, reflecting back to the same person); indefinite pronouns (list including someone, everybody, everything, none); demonstrative pronouns (this/that/these/those, also usable as adjectives/determiners); unclear pronoun reference ('Lizzie ... she broke it'); I/me and who/whom mix-ups. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Using Pronouns Clearly
sourceRecords.provider: Purdue Online Writing Lab, Purdue University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: a pronoun refers to a noun or takes its place; pronouns must agree in number (plural antecedent takes plural pronoun); pronouns must refer clearly to a specific noun, with the classic vague it/they/this/which examples; the note that they/their is increasingly used as a singular, gender-neutral pronoun recognized by AP and Chicago Manual of Style. The page restricts reproduction; used reference-only with original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Pronoun Case
sourceRecords.provider: Purdue Online Writing Lab, Purdue University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: three pronoun cases — subjective (pronouns used as subjects), objective (pronouns used as objects of verbs or prepositions), and possessive (pronouns expressing ownership) — with the full form table (I/me/my(mine), you/you/your(yours), he,she,it/him,her,it/his,her(hers),it(its), we/us/our(ours), they/them/their(theirs)). The page restricts reproduction; used reference-only with original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Reflexive Pronouns
sourceRecords.provider: Purdue Online Writing Lab, Purdue University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: a reflexive pronoun is used for the object of a verb when it refers to the same noun as the subject; reflexive forms end in -self or -selves; when subject and object are the same, use the reflexive, otherwise do not; the improper-use example 'email Bob or myself' versus correct 'email Bob or me'. The page restricts reproduction; used reference-only with original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Relative pronouns (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.provider: Cambridge Dictionary, Cambridge University Press & Assessment
sourceRecords.notes: Reputable publisher reference (Tier B-equivalent). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: relative pronouns introduce relative clauses; the most common are who, whom, whose, which, that; who for people (and sometimes pet animals), which for animals and things, that for people, animals, and things (informal). Used only to name relative pronouns as clause connectors; clause structure itself is deferred to the sentence-structure sibling topic. Reference-only; no source wording reproduced.
